newsitem.title: ZAIRE: Zaire PM under fire over war, rivals plot downfall.
newsitem.headline: Zaire PM under fire over war, rivals plot downfall.

text.p: Zaire's part-Tutsi prime minister, Kengo wa Dondo, architect of Western-backed economic reforms in the corruption-plagued nation, is in the firing line over a Tutsi revolt in the east.

Denounced in street protests as being soft on Tutsi-led Rwanda, his main opposition rivals say they have opened talks with supporters of ailing and absentee president Mobutu Sese Seko on forming a government of national unity to replace him.

"The two political families, that of Etienne Tshisekedi and that of Mobutu, have established contact and we may very soon see a government of national unity," Tshisekedi spokesman Mukendi wa Mulumba told Reuters on Sunday.
"If President Mobutu dies the two political familes will have to reach a consensus in parliament on who should govern in the interim," he added. Tshisekedi was prime minister in 1992-3.
On Saturday, the usually reticent army chief of staff General Eluki Monga said publicly that Kengo and his government had not done enough to help the troops at the battlefront.
"We regret that the government is moving too slowly and has not yet given us the necessary means," he said in Kinshasa.
Kengo, who has shown himself to be an astute political player in the past, has opted for a business as usual approach.

"When a war starts people look for a scapegoat," he told reporters after Friday's protests. "Today it happens to be the prime minister and his government, but I will continue to work without listening to malicious gossip."

But political pundits say that the entry of the army into the political fray could well herald the beginning of the end for Kengo, who was voted into office as a compromise candidate by Zaire's transitional assembly in 1994.
"This time it looks serious. The fact that it is the army that's saying this could well be used as a justification to remove the prime minister," one said.
"We still don't know where Mobutu stands," he added.

Mobutu, who seized power in 1965 and ruled virtually unchallenged until 1990 when foreign and domestic pressure forced him to embrace democratic reform, has been in Switzerland since undergoing surgery for prostate cancer there in August.

Kengo's economic reforms, resented by some generals and many of Mobutu's placemen who found themselves targeted, helped raise Mobutu's profile in the West -- where he was accused of human rights abuses and corruption and treated as a virtual pariah.

In the past, Kengo has neutralised any challenge with the support of the veteran strongman, who remains Zaire's sole symbol of national unity and whose supporters enjoy a majority in the transitional assembly.
As prime minister elected by a national conference in 1992, Tshisekedi was shunted aside in favour of a Mobutu appointee in 1993. He bitterly refuses to accept Kengo's 1994 election.
Zaire has had six other transitional prime ministers.
Kengo, whose mother was part Tutsi and father was Polish, has lasted longer than any but this time he has to reckon with a wave of anti-Rwandan and particularly anti-Tutsi feeling.
Mobs have attacked Tutsi shops and homes, hundreds of Tutsis who figured prominently in Kinshasa's business and professional communities have fled.
Kengo has taken a firm line on Rwanda, denouncing it as an invader and refusing the attend peace talks.
But the transitional parliament, which summoned him to explain his conduct of the war publicly, later recommended that anyone of Tutsi origin employed by the state should be sacked.
Overhanging everything is Mobutu's illness and his own haunting prophecy that without "the guide" -- as he likes to be known -- the sprawling Central African state will collapse.
The armed forces are divided into units with varying degrees of training, equipment and pay. Mobutu is commander-in-chief.
"If the president had been here the government would not have moved slowly to provide for the war," said Eluki.
Mukendi played down speculation of a coup, saying neither Zaire's people nor the international community would allow it.
"The truth is nobody here really knows the state of the president's health and that may make it hard for any army officer to take over on his own behalf," a Western diplomat said.
"If someone tried by himself and did not succeed there could be very serious trouble," the diplomat added.
